title: The Dali Trick
author: Jonny Thomson
summary: Jonny Thomson opens with a story about a university student named Ben who adopted an alter ego -- a more confident, assertive version of himself he could inhabit in seminars and presentations -- and traces the philosophical lineage of this instinct from Dali's deliberate construction of the persona 'Avida Dollars' (an anagram of Salvador Dali) to Goffman's dramaturgical theory to Sartre's account of the gaze. The philosophical core of the article is Goffman's claim in The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life: all public interaction is already performance in the sense that we manage impressions, regulate disclosure, and present context-appropriate versions of ourselves in every social encounter -- the question is not whether you are performing but how consciously and skillfully. Sartre's gaze is introduced as the phenomenological root of this: the moment you are seen by another consciousness, you become an object in their world and must construct a response, which is always a kind of performance. Thomson introduces the Batman Effect study as empirical support for what the philosophers described: children given a Batman persona to inhabit persisted longer on tedious tasks than children who worked as themselves, because the costume created psychological distance from the frustration. The practical application Thomson extracts is not a performance tip but a philosophical reorientation: instead of asking 'Who am I, really?' before entering a difficult room, ask 'Who do I want to be in this room?' -- a question that treats identity as something to construct rather than unearth.
points: Dali's 'Avida Dollars' persona was a deliberate philosophical construction: a third-person self that could absorb public attention, strategic eccentricity, and commercial contradiction without destabilizing the private person.

Goffman's dramaturgical theory establishes that all social interaction is already impression management -- the choice is not between authentic and performed but between unconscious and deliberate performance.

Sartre's gaze is the phenomenological root: the moment another consciousness perceives you, you become an object in their world and must construct a response, which is always a form of self-presentation.

The Batman Effect demonstrates empirically what Goffman described philosophically: children who inhabited a given persona persisted significantly longer on difficult tasks than children who worked as themselves.

The reorientation Thomson offers is practical: ask 'Who do I want to be in this room?' rather than 'Who am I, really?' -- treating identity as something constructed for context rather than excavated from a stable interior.
quotes: Dali did not stumble into eccentricity. He engineered it. 'Avida Dollars' was a persona he put on and took off -- a third-person self that could absorb the contradictions of fame, commerce, and artistic seriousness without requiring him to resolve them privately.

Goffman's insight is not cynical. It is descriptive. Every time you enter a room, you are already managing an impression, already regulating what you disclose, already presenting a version of yourself calibrated to the context. The question is not whether you perform. It is how consciously.

Sartre's gaze is the philosophical root of all this. The moment another consciousness perceives you, you are no longer just a subject having experiences. You are an object in their world. You must construct a response to being seen. That construction is always, in some sense, a performance.

The Batman Effect is remarkable because it confirms the philosophical intuition experimentally. Children told to pretend they were Batman while doing a tedious task persisted significantly longer than children who worked as themselves. The persona created distance from frustration. The costume was not a disguise. It was a tool.

Stop asking 'Who am I, really?' before you walk into the difficult room. Start asking 'Who do I want to be in this room?' That is not inauthenticity. That is agency over the version of yourself that gets to show up.
